memoryText: The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Spend your time with the memory verse. Read Job 1:21 slowly, three times, and then close your Bible and say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the review of the week, and choose one of the three questions to write about or to talk over with someone you trust.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Job 1:21 is the confession of a man who has just lost everything. It is short enough to carry in your head, and heavy enough that it will take a lifetime to learn.

“The LORD gave.” Job begins with gratitude. He has not forgotten what he received. The children, the land, the livestock, and the health were all gifts, and he names them as gifts. Everything good in your life is a gift too, and gratitude is the first step in learning to worship.

“And the LORD has taken away.” This is the hard part, and Job does not soften it. He does not say that Satan took away, or that raiders took away, though both are true in the story. He sees through the second causes to the sovereign God who permits them. He does not say that God is guilty. He says that God is God. This is one of the most mature statements in Scripture, and it is not easy to say.

“Blessed be the name of the LORD.” The verse does not stop with the loss. It ends with praise, and the praise is aimed at the same LORD who gave and took. Job is not praising loss. He is praising the one who is greater than loss.

For the Christian, this verse takes on a new shape in light of the cross. The Father gave his Son, and the Son was taken away, and yet in that giving and taking is the greatest blessing in history. Job could not see that yet. You can.
weekInReview: This week you began Unit 4 and the book of Job. You were taken behind the curtain into heaven, where Satan accused Job and God set a limit on what he could do. You watched Job lose his children and his wealth and his health, and you heard him worship. You read two laments, Psalm 10 and Psalm 13, which gave you words for the question “Where are you, LORD?” and the question “How long?” Then the friends arrived. You heard Eliphaz suggest that Job’s suffering must be the result of sin, and Bildad go further and say that Job’s children had earned their deaths. Job answered with grief, with bitterness, and with the first stirrings of a longing for a mediator. The week taught that suffering is not a verdict, and that faithful people are allowed to ask hard questions.
reflectionQuestions: Job lost almost everything, and he worshiped. Is there something you have lost, or are afraid of losing, that you need to place again in God’s hands? Write down what it is, and then write “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” beside it.

How does Job’s longing for an “arbiter” who could stand between him and God (9:33) point you to Christ? Think about what it means that Jesus has laid his hand on both God and humanity. What would Job say if he could see the cross?
Which of Job’s friends do you most resemble when someone you love is hurting? What would it look like this week to sit silently with someone instead of offering explanations?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for what he has given, and place in his hands what you fear to lose.
Thank Jesus, the mediator Job longed for.
Rest in his care as the week ends.
